enc.title: Covalent bond: what if the atoms move apart, or differ?
enc.intro: Two atoms, one orbital each, at the same level $\epsilon$. An electron can hop between them with amplitude $t$, which falls off exponentially with distance because it comes from the overlap of the two orbitals. The $2\times2$ problem has eigenvalues $E_\mp=\epsilon\mp t$: a bonding level (density piled up between the atoms) and an antibonding one (node in the middle). The slider $d$ is the atom separation; the toggle makes the atoms different, with level mismatch $\Delta$, which turns a covalent bond into an ionic one.
tasks: Predict first: halve the overlap (move the atoms apart). Does the splitting $2t$ grow or shrink, and what happens to it as $d\to\infty$? Then check on the plot.
Two electrons fill the bonding level. Read off the energy gain at $d_0$. Why does the total energy have a minimum at all (what does the core repulsion do)?
Switch on 'unequal atoms' with $\Delta\gg t$: what happens to the weights of the bonding orbital on the two atoms, and to the splitting $\sqrt{t^2+\Delta^2/4}$? Which bond type is this?
Remove the 'tight-binding' bonding by setting $d$ large: why does each atom end up neutral with one electron (and not with two in the lower level)?

enc.title: One Fermi gas, three systems: copper, white dwarf, neutron star
enc.intro: A gas of spin-1/2 fermions at density $n$ fills momentum states up to $k_F=(3\pi^2n)^{1/3}$. The density slider $n$ moves along the horizontal axis of a log-log chart of $E_F$; the temperature slider sets the green line $k_BT$. If $k_BT\ll E_F$ the gas is degenerate: the Pauli principle, not heat, gives the pressure $P\approx\frac25nE_F$. At $p_F=mc$ (yellow line) the electrons turn relativistic and $E_F\propto n^{1/3}$ instead of $n^{2/3}$, which is what produces the Chandrasekhar limit.
tasks: Set $n=8.47\times10^{28}$ m$^{-3}$ (copper) and predict $E_F$ and $T_F$ before reading them (about 7.0 eV and $8\times10^4$ K). Is copper degenerate at 300 K? By how many orders of magnitude?
Predict first: by what factor does $E_F$ change if $n$ grows by $10^3$ (non-relativistic)? Check against the chart, then find the density where the curves bend (yellow line).
White dwarf core: is $T=10^7$ K above or below $T_F$? Estimate $T/T_F$ and say why the star does not shrink when it cools.
Neutron star: the same formulas with $m\to m_n$. Compare $E_F$ of the neutrons with the rest energy $m_nc^2=940$ MeV and decide whether they are relativistic.

source.where: Ch. 3.1 (pp. 66-76), eqs. 3.1-3.33 free electron gas, Fermi energy

enc.title: Nearly free electrons: switch the lattice potential on
enc.intro: Free electrons have $E=\hbar^2k^2/2m$. A crystal only knows $k$ modulo $G=2\pi/a$, so the parabola is folded into the first Brillouin zone $[-\pi/a,\pi/a]$ and the folded branches cross at the zone edge and centre. A weak periodic potential with Fourier component $U_G$ mixes the two degenerate waves $k$ and $k-G$; the exact $2\times2$ solution splits them by $2|U_G|$: a band gap. The slider $|U_G|$ is the strength of the lattice potential, $a$ is the lattice constant (a larger $a$ lowers the zone-edge energy $E_0$), and the electron count decides which bands are full.
tasks: Predict first: with $U_G=0$ what do the folded bands look like and is there a gap? Then switch $U_G$ on and read the gap at $k=\pi/a$ (expect $2|U_G|$).
Which of the two electron counts per cell (1, 2) gives an insulator in 1D, and what is the reason (two electrons per band, one band fills the zone)?
Look at the curvature at the band edge: why is the effective mass of the upper band light and that of the lower band negative? Reduce $U_G$ and see how $m^*$ scales.
Increase $a$ at fixed $U_G$: how do $E_0$ and the ratio $E_0/|U_G|$ change, and why do the free-electron results become better?

source.where: Ch. 3.2 (pp. 77-87), Bloch theorem, nearly free electrons

enc.title: Ewald construction: which reciprocal points light up?
enc.intro: Elastic scattering conserves $|\mathbf k|$: $\mathbf k'=\mathbf k+\mathbf G$ with $|\mathbf k'|=|\mathbf k|$ (Laue condition). In the picture, the reciprocal lattice (grey dots, spacing $2\pi/a$ and $2\pi/b$) is fixed; the blue circle of radius $|k|=2\pi/\lambda$ is centred at $-\mathbf k$ and passes through the origin. Every reciprocal point on the circle is a diffraction peak, with the scattering angle $2\theta$ printed. Slider $\lambda$ is the circle radius, the angle slider is the orientation of the crystal relative to the beam.
tasks: Predict first: for $\lambda>2a$ (the circle is smaller than half the lattice spacing in reciprocal space), are there any peaks other than the direct beam? Explain with $2d\sin\theta=n\lambda$.
Choose $\lambda=0.8a$ and rotate the angle until the $(1,0)$ point lights up: check $\sin\theta=\lambda/2d$ with $2\theta$ as printed.
Switch to a rectangular lattice $b=1.5a$: which points move closer to the origin, and why do reflections along $y$ appear at longer $\lambda$?
Link to the HS23 neutron problem: for fixed $\lambda$, what is the largest $|\mathbf G|$ that can ever contribute (circle diameter $2|k|$)?

source.where: Ch. 1.5 (pp. 15-23), Bragg and Laue, Ewald sphere
